item.title: n8n saved me more time this year than any AI tool, and most of my workflows don't use AI at all
item.itunes:title: n8n saved me more time this year than any AI tool, and most of my workflows don't use AI at all
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Before I started using n8n, most of my automations were Python or Bash scripts that ran through cron jobs. They got things done, although adding something new or figuring out why a script stopped working took more effort than I wanted. I only have a working knowledge of Python, and even when an AI tool helps me write the code, I still have to understand enough of it to maintain the automation. With n8n, I can follow the workflow on a canvas, check what each step does, and change the part I need.

I now use it for everything from managing my files to running automations around my house, and it has saved me more time this year than any AI tool I’ve tried. Most of those workflows, like checking a calendar, filtering emails, or deciding what happens when a sensor changes state, come down to rules and don’t even need AI.

I spend less time building and fixing automations

n8n makes it easier to manage automations

To show you how easy it is to build and manage automations with n8n, let’s look at one of the automations I have on my website. I have a contact form workflow that collects new inquiries via a webhook and then creates a task in Notion using the submitted information. Both ends of that process are visible on the canvas, and I can open either node to change its settings or check the data passing through it. When I need something more specific, I can add a little code, as I do to format dates in this workflow.

You can build the same thing in Python, of course. However, you also need to handle connections to those services, process their responses, and decide how you’ll know when something fails. You can use cron for scheduling a script, but everything that happens after it starts depends on what you’ve written. n8n already provides much of that functionality through its integrations and workflow controls. I can add a condition, connect another application, or change where the output goes without having to work through the entire script.

That becomes very useful when an automation stops working. n8n's execution view shows which node failed, the information it received, and the error it returned. You can load that execution’s data into the editor, make a change, and test it against the input that caused the problem. I find that much easier than debugging code I’ve partly relied on an AI tool to write.

4 cool automations I can pull off using my self-hosted n8n server

If you're willing to master this complex app, n8n can help you automate every aspect of your life

By  Ayush Pande

My home automations are easier to change

You can pair Home Assistant with n8n

n8n also makes it easier to build and manage home automations, especially when you want a routine to do more than respond to a single trigger. Home Assistant brings your devices together and gives you an automation editor, but you can also connect it to n8n and build your workflows there. You get the same visual canvas to connect devices, check conditions, and bring in other applications.

The built-in Home Assistant node means you don’t need to write an integration yourself. It can read device states and call services to control lights, switches, and other devices. Home Assistant can also send events to an n8n webhook to start a workflow. For example, it can detect movement and send that information to n8n, which can check the time, room temperature, and calendar before deciding what to do. The same event can lead to different actions depending on the conditions you set.

The editor becomes particularly useful as you add more branches. You can connect each condition to the relevant action and follow the paths across the canvas. You’re also able to connect home automations to services outside Home Assistant. For example, a calendar event can start a routine before a meeting, or device readings can go into a spreadsheet or scheduled report.

Most of these workflows have no reason to use AI

AI is completely optional

I’ve built n8n workflows that use AI to classify emails and extract expense details from messages. They are useful when the input changes and the workflow needs to understand what someone wrote. However, a lot of the things I automate already have clear conditions. If I add a model to the fix, I'll also have to configure prompts and handle its responses, which I can express through a couple of checks.

The home automations are a good example. You don't need AI to check whether someone is home, whether a window is open, or whether a meeting started before a certain time. You can combine several of these conditions into a fairly elaborate routine without asking a model to interpret anything.

Email cleanup works similarly. My earlier inbox assistant uses AI for contextual classification, but you don’t need that just to clear old newsletters or organize notifications from known senders. You can use an n8n workflow to search for messages using their sender, labels, and age, then archive the matches. Gmail’s own filters cover basic incoming-mail rules, and n8n gives you room to combine scheduled cleanup with actions in other applications.

n8n has been a lifesaver

I can use Python to automate things, and I can use n8n, but the latter is extremely easy to use and lets me build and manage complex automations even if I don’t know how to code. I’ll admit that building Python automations is easy, especially now that you can use a coding agent to write the code for you. But when you don’t know how to code, maintaining those automations becomes a challenge, even with AI managing them. I’ve noticed that I often get stuck in a loop trying to fix code because I have no clue what’s going on.

I thought Google Tasks was basic, then I paired it with Gemini

Supercharged Google Tasks with AI

By  Parth Shah

item.title: Microsoft's "Project Odeon" may turn Windows 11's Settings into a Microsoft Store app
item.itunes:title: Microsoft's "Project Odeon" may turn Windows 11's Settings into a Microsoft Store app
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Project Odeon makes Settings a Microsoft Store app so Microsoft can update it outside Windows Update.
  • Found in an Insider branch as a Store entry; it coexists with the current Settings app for now.
  • Store-based Settings could speed moving Control Panel features into Settings without holding up Windows Update.

Microsoft has quite a few projects going right now. The biggest one is Windows K2, which sounds like a brand-new version of the operating system, but it's actually a major revamp of Windows 11 to tweak users' biggest pain points. There's also Project Helix, which will define the next generation of Xbox consoles

Now, a report has come in claiming that there's another one: Project Odeon. This one seemingly turns the Settings panel into a Windows Store app, which should allow Microsoft to tweak features without waiting around for a Windows Update to go out.

Project Odeon seemingly turns the Windows 11 Settings panel into a Microsoft Store app

Not much has been confirmed as of yet

The claim comes to us via Windows Latest, which discovered the feature in a Windows 11 Insider branch. It spotted a new entry on the Microsoft Store titled "Project Odeon" which shared the same icon as Windows 11's Settings panel. When downloaded, Project Odeon didn't overwrite the Settings panel, and it was possible to open them side-by-side. However, it's likely Microsoft chose this behavior because Project Odeon is still a WIP and is missing a ton of settings, so people still need access to the default Settings app to tweak specific things.

So, what's Microsoft's big plan with Project Odeon? In my opinion, I believe this will become a full replacement for Settings. Microsoft has been trying to move all of Control Panel over to Settings for a while; we've been reporting it for over two years now. There's a chance that the reason it's taking so long is that additions to Settings need to hitch a ride on Windows Update, which may be complicating things.

By going for a Microsoft Store-based approach, Microsoft can send out updates and new features without being tied up with Windows Update. I'd imagine Microsoft would use this avenue to add Control Panel features to Settings, and then remove said features from Control Panel during a standard Windows Update. That way, people can move over to the new Settings panel more quickly, allowing Microsoft to slowly dismantle the Control Panel without denying users a way to toggle specific settings.

5 reasons the Windows 11 Settings app makes me forget about the Control Panel

The Control Panel is old news

item.title: The triple-OS NexPhone runs Android, Linux, and Windows 11, but you’ll have to wait until 2027 for it
item.itunes:title: The triple-OS NexPhone runs Android, Linux, and Windows 11, but you’ll have to wait until 2027 for it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • NexPhone will dual-boot Android, Debian Linux, and Windows 11 on a single handset.
  • Shipping for the NexPhone has been delayed to March 2027 (end of Q1) after 14 years in development.
  • New preorders will cost $599, but people who preordered at the original $549 won't need to pay extra.

Usually, you're only stuck with one OS on your phone, but what if you could pick between Android, Linux, and Windows 11? It sounds ambitious, but that's a major selling point for NexPhone, which has been in the works for 14 years now. The phone was originally scheduled to release later this year, but unfortunately, it has been pushed back a few months.

The NexPhone has been delayed until March 2027

What's a few more months compared to 14 years, though?

If you've never heard of it, the NexPhone is designed to run Android, Linux (specifically, Debian), and Windows 11 on a dual-boot. It has been in the works for a long time now; in fact, that video just above was posted all the way back in 2012. It was originally pencilled in to release in late 2026, but that has been pushed back. As per an updated statement on the NexPhone website:

Our estimated shipping window is now the end of Q1 2027 (March 2027). New preorders are priced at $599, and the device price remains protected for customers who reserved at either $549 or $599. NexPhone is now running Android 17 on development devices, with continued Linux and Windows development.

I'm not sure how they're going to squeeze all of that functionality into a $599 phone, but I'm more than willing to check it out when it releases. You can reserve your own on the NexPhone website if you're as interested as I am.

item.title: The Apple Magic Keyboard Folio is down to its best price in two years
item.itunes:title: The Apple Magic Keyboard Folio is down to its best price in two years
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Ever thought about taking your iPad to the next level? The Apple Magic Keyboard Folio will do just that. It's a cover that protects your iPad and, more importantly, adds a keyboard and trackpad. Now, while this might seem like a pretty simple accessory, Apple charges an excessive amount, with a retail price of $249. We wouldn't dare spend that much, but luckily it's now 40% off on Amazon, at $150. This is the best price we've seen for this in the past two years. Get it now before it's gone.

Apple Magic Keyboard Folio for iPad 10

If you want a detachable keyboard, you can't go wrong with Apple's Magic Keyboard. It includes a keyboard, trackpad, and a USB Type-C port. It also attaches to the iPad magnetically. While it's not the most protective case out there, it does turn your iPad into something closer to a laptop.

See at Amazon

Steep price but it's nice

Credit: Apple

It's hard to imagine paying so much for a keyboard accessory for an iPad, but Apple does make one of the best ones available. Sure, you can go with one from Logitech or another major brand, but it just doesn't work the same. The keys feel good, and the trackpad is just like what you'd get on a laptop.

Now, iPadOS has gone through a few updates over the past years that really enhances the productivity aspect of the product. The best part about the Magic Keyboard Folio is that you don't have to charge it. You just connect it to your iPad and you're good to go. The Smart Connector handles both power and data.

This particular model is compatible with the iPad A16 and 10th Generation models. It has a full keyboard and function keys at the top. There's no backlighting though, but we think the screen should provide enough illumination if you need to work in dark environments. Just act quickly because this deal won't be around for long.

item.title: Someone actually ported the original Halo to the N64, and it’s as wild as it sounds
item.itunes:title: Someone actually ported the original Halo to the N64, and it’s as wild as it sounds
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Halo: Combat Evolved has been rebuilt to run on Nintendo 64, complete with split-screen 4-player multiplayer and Firefight.
  • The game uses the halo-ce-universal decompilation to recompile objects, physics, HUD, and a new renderer for the N64 VR4300.
  • The port features 13 recreated maps, including Blood Gulch and Battle Creek.

The retro game decompilation/recompilation port world keeps getting wilder. This latest port is maybe the weirdest I've seen so far: someone has actually gotten Halo: Combat Evolved running on the Nintendo 64.

It's the type of port that doesn't need to exist and looks awful, but you probably still want to see what the heck it actually looks like and how it plays. Halo 64 is the OG Xbox Halo: Combat Evolved remade for the N64, complete with the Nintendo console's signature blocky graphics and plenty of aliasing.

This isn't a port of the iconic first-person shooter's campaign; it's a multiplayer experience that supports up to four players locally via split-screen. It even includes a Firefight mode that spawns waves of enemies for players to fight.

Like other recent Halo ports, including the browser-based port and the Windows 11, Linux, PS5, and Android ports, this project is based on the halo-ce-universal decompilation project. Halo 64 takes Halo: Combat Evolved's objects, physics, weapons, game type, HUD, and more, and compiles them for the N64's VR4300 CPU, along with a new renderer.

Halo 64 is playable right now and includes a lot of Halo: CE's key features

The retro FPS just got even more old school

Credit: JackTulli

13 of the game's maps have been recreated for Halo 64, including iconic arenas like Battle Creek, Sidewinder, Wizard, Prisoner, and, of course, Blood Gulch. All the familiar vehicles and weapons are in every map, too.

The wacky port also includes familiar game types, including Slayer, Team Slayer, Slayer Pro, Capture the Flag, King of the Hill, and more. Oh, and there are bots, a feature the original Halo: Combat Evolved didn't even include.

I haven't tried Halo 64 myself yet, but it's a pretty impressive project, and despite the rudimentary visuals, it still has that OG Halo vibe. Like all recompilations, you need a Halo disc image to play the game, which you can dump from your own copy or acquire elsewhere.

Credit: JackTulli

Like so many retro ports dropping lately, Claude obviously helped significantly with Halo 64's creation. Still, it's a fascinating project and a good example of a weird port that probably wouldn't exist without AI vibe coding. You can download the game directly from its GitHub page.

You can now play the original Halo for free in your browser with 128-player multiplayer

Activision may have taken over the Halo series, but at least you can play the OG game in a browser now.

item.title: Two days after release, Total War: Shogun 2 Complete Edition gets pulled from Steam for quality issues
item.itunes:title: Two days after release, Total War: Shogun 2 Complete Edition gets pulled from Steam for quality issues
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Sega pulled Total War: Shogun 2 - Complete Edition from Steam over bugs and alleged AI-upscaled assets.
  • The original Shogun 2 was restored on Steam, and existing owners can still play while issues are investigated.
  • Review-bombing pushed the Complete Edition to 'Overwhelmingly Negative' and spilled over to the original Shogun 2 Steam page.

Two days ago, we reported on how Total War: Shogun 2's Complete Edition was getting review-bombed after people discovered brand new bugs and alleged AI-upscaled assets. The backlash was so strong that the title earned an "Overwhelmingly Negative" review score, with only 19% of the reviews being positive. Well, it seems Sega recognises that its fanbase has a point, as it has removed Total War: Shogun 2 - Complete Edition from Steam until it fixes the problems.

Total War: Shogun 2 - Complete Edition is removed from Steam for quality issues

It should be back once it's ready

Credit: Creative Assembly

As The Verge reported, Sega announced on Steam that Total War: Shogun 2 - Complete Edition was removed from the storefront just two days after its release. The game publisher cites issues with the title as its main reason, echoing what people were criticising in the reviews:

We’re aware that Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards. We’ve seen your feedback, comments, and reviews. We agree that the current experience is not where it needs to be.

As a result we are working with platform holders to remove the game from sale and to reinstate the original game while we investigate the issues. Existing owners will still be able to access and play the game.

The good news is that the original version of Total War: Shogun 2 has returned to the storefront after the publisher removed it to make way for the complete edition. The bad news is that criticism for the complete edition has spilled over into Shogun 2's reviews, with people bringing the score down to "Mixed" and expressing disdain for how the company handled the remaster.

Yeah, that will definitely affect user reception somewhat.

item.title: Your Proxmox VM is probably emulating hardware that hasn't existed for decades
item.itunes:title: Your Proxmox VM is probably emulating hardware that hasn't existed for decades
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Every time you spin up a virtual machine in Proxmox, the creation wizard makes a stop at the System tab that most people just click straight through. One of the fields there is Machine, and unless you change it manually, it defaults to i440fx, which tells QEMU to build your VM around emulating an Intel chipset from the 90s. Intel's 440FX chipset launched in 1996 for the Pentium Pro, and there is a much more modern option in the list, so why doesn't Proxmox use it?

It sounds like a problem, but it's not really a concern. The machine type is your VM’s virtual motherboard, and Proxmox defaults to i440FX because it’s the safe, compatible choice. Once you know what it actually controls, you’ll know when to leave it alone and when to pick something newer, which isn't all that often.

I tried using a Proxmox-based Windows 11 VM as my daily driver - here's how it went

All it took was a little bit of tinkering and a whole lot of patience

12
By  Ayush Pande

What machine type actually controls in Proxmox VMs

Proxmox's forgotten VM setting

The machine type dropdown selects the hardware layout of your VM's virtual motherboard. When a guest operating system boots, it finds a chipset, a set of buses, and a handful of built-in controllers, and the machine type dictates what all of those are.

It's easy to confuse with the settings you find around it, like the CPU type, which decides which processor features the guest can see, or the firmware setting, which chooses between SeaBIOS and OVMF. Your disk controller and network card are devices plugged into the virtual board, and the machine type is the board itself, so changing it is like keeping the same processor, memory, and drives but swapping the motherboard underneath them.

The 440FX that's the default inside Proxmox gives the guest a host bridge, an ISA bridge, an IDE controller, a USB controller, and an ACPI power-management device, all sitting on a conventional PCI bus. There’s no PCI Express anywhere on it, and you can confirm this yourself by running lspci in a Linux VM, where the first few entries list the chipset’s parts by their original Intel names.

My outdated Windows 10 PC was headed for the recycling bin until Proxmox gave it a second life

This dinosaur machine now runs my LLMs inside an LXC

4
By  Ayush Pande

Why a chipset from 1996 isn't making your VM slow

It doesn't have Pentium Pro-era performance

If your VM is built on a Pentium Pro-era board, you might expect it to perform like one, but the chipset has very little to do with performance in a VM.

Your guest’s code runs on your host’s processor through KVM, and the CPU type only controls which instruction-set features are exposed to the guest. The wizard’s default, x86-64-v2-AES, targets Intel CPUs from the Westmere generation onward, far newer than anything a real 440FX ever hosted. QEMU just reproduces the chipset’s layout, not its limitations, so there’s no 1996-era bus speed throttling your VM.

Storage and networking are where performance lives, and Proxmox recommends handling both with VirtIO. Rather than imitating a real disk controller or network card, a VirtIO device cooperates with the hypervisor directly, which is much faster than emulating legacy hardware. VirtIO SCSI single has been the default disk controller for new Linux VMs since Proxmox VE 7.3. These devices plug into the virtual PCI bus like any other card, so the age of the chipset around them barely registers.

4 reasons why I'll stick with Proxmox even though the free version of ESXi is back

Why switch to ESXi again when Proxmox is just that good?

6
By  Ayush Pande

Where the i440FX does hold you back

Handing physical devices from the host to the VM

The other option in the Machine dropdown is Q35, which emulates Intel’s Q35 Express chipset and ICH9 southbridge from 2007. That’s hardly cutting-edge, but it brings one thing i440FX can’t: a virtual PCI Express bus.

That matters most for passthrough, where you hand a physical device in your host, like a GPU, directly to a VM. Proxmox’s option to present a passed-through device on a PCIe port only works with Q35, and plain PCI isn't going to cut it here. Passthrough isn’t impossible on i440FX, but devices show up there as conventional PCI cards, which doesn’t work for every guest or driver, and if you're planning on passing through a GPU, Q35 is definitely the better starting point.

Q35 is also required for Intel’s flavor of emulated IOMMU. Additionally, it's what the Proxmox wizard selects automatically when you set the guest OS to Windows 11, along with UEFI firmware and a TPM. If you’ve built a Windows 11 VM, you may already be running Q35 without realizing it.

Steam streaming on Proxmox doesn't require GPU passthrough, and my LXC setup proves it

It's not as weird as it sounds, honest

7
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Why you shouldn't flip every VM to Q35

It's not always necessary

With all of that in mind, it's tempting to open every VM you run and switch it over now, but you shouldn't. At least, not without a plan as to why.

On Linux, the usual casualty is networking in an active VM. Most modern distributions name network interfaces based on where they sit on the bus, and that changes with the new layout. An interface called ens18 can come back as something like enp6s18, and if your network configuration still points at the old name, the VM boots without an IP address. Windows can be fussier still and may need repair work after the switch, and while neither is really hard to fix, both are annoying on a VM that was working fine beforehand.

That's probably why Proxmox hasn't changed the default, because a VM without an explicit type set just uses the default, so changing it would just swap every VM that was created without one.

I built a $15 ESP32 display that shows exactly what my home server is doing

The missing piece wasn’t another monitor.

By  Shekhar Vaidya

Leave the machine type alone unless you need it

Seeing a 1996 chipset in your VM’s settings is a little jarring, but i440FX isn’t Proxmox neglecting to update a dropdown or a hefty performance sacrifice in the name of compatibility. It is for the sake of compatibility, but it works best out of the box for virtually all operating systems, and the parts that matter for performance have nothing to do with the VM's chipset.

Every time you spin up a virtual machine in Proxmox, the creation wizard makes a stop at the System tab that most people just click straight through. One of the fields there is Machine, and unless you change it manually, it defaults to i440fx, which tells QEMU to build your VM around emulating an Intel chipset from the 90s. Intel's 440FX chipset launched in 1996 for the Pentium Pro, and there is a much more modern option in the list, so why doesn't Proxmox use it?

It sounds like a problem, but it's not really a concern. The machine type is your VM’s virtual motherboard, and Proxmox defaults to i440FX because it’s the safe, compatible choice. Once you know what it actually controls, you’ll know when to leave it alone and when to pick something newer, which isn't all that often.

I tried using a Proxmox-based Windows 11 VM as my daily driver - here's how it went

All it took was a little bit of tinkering and a whole lot of patience

12
By  Ayush Pande

What machine type actually controls in Proxmox VMs

Proxmox's forgotten VM setting

The machine type dropdown selects the hardware layout of your VM's virtual motherboard. When a guest operating system boots, it finds a chipset, a set of buses, and a handful of built-in controllers, and the machine type dictates what all of those are.

It's easy to confuse with the settings you find around it, like the CPU type, which decides which processor features the guest can see, or the firmware setting, which chooses between SeaBIOS and OVMF. Your disk controller and network card are devices plugged into the virtual board, and the machine type is the board itself, so changing it is like keeping the same processor, memory, and drives but swapping the motherboard underneath them.

The 440FX that's the default inside Proxmox gives the guest a host bridge, an ISA bridge, an IDE controller, a USB controller, and an ACPI power-management device, all sitting on a conventional PCI bus. There’s no PCI Express anywhere on it, and you can confirm this yourself by running lspci in a Linux VM, where the first few entries list the chipset’s parts by their original Intel names.

My outdated Windows 10 PC was headed for the recycling bin until Proxmox gave it a second life

This dinosaur machine now runs my LLMs inside an LXC

4
By  Ayush Pande

Why a chipset from 1996 isn't making your VM slow

It doesn't have Pentium Pro-era performance

If your VM is built on a Pentium Pro-era board, you might expect it to perform like one, but the chipset has very little to do with performance in a VM.

Your guest’s code runs on your host’s processor through KVM, and the CPU type only controls which instruction-set features are exposed to the guest. The wizard’s default, x86-64-v2-AES, targets Intel CPUs from the Westmere generation onward, far newer than anything a real 440FX ever hosted. QEMU just reproduces the chipset’s layout, not its limitations, so there’s no 1996-era bus speed throttling your VM.

Storage and networking are where performance lives, and Proxmox recommends handling both with VirtIO. Rather than imitating a real disk controller or network card, a VirtIO device cooperates with the hypervisor directly, which is much faster than emulating legacy hardware. VirtIO SCSI single has been the default disk controller for new Linux VMs since Proxmox VE 7.3. These devices plug into the virtual PCI bus like any other card, so the age of the chipset around them barely registers.

4 reasons why I'll stick with Proxmox even though the free version of ESXi is back

Why switch to ESXi again when Proxmox is just that good?

6
By  Ayush Pande

Where the i440FX does hold you back

Handing physical devices from the host to the VM

The other option in the Machine dropdown is Q35, which emulates Intel’s Q35 Express chipset and ICH9 southbridge from 2007. That’s hardly cutting-edge, but it brings one thing i440FX can’t: a virtual PCI Express bus.

That matters most for passthrough, where you hand a physical device in your host, like a GPU, directly to a VM. Proxmox’s option to present a passed-through device on a PCIe port only works with Q35, and plain PCI isn't going to cut it here. Passthrough isn’t impossible on i440FX, but devices show up there as conventional PCI cards, which doesn’t work for every guest or driver, and if you're planning on passing through a GPU, Q35 is definitely the better starting point.

Q35 is also required for Intel’s flavor of emulated IOMMU. Additionally, it's what the Proxmox wizard selects automatically when you set the guest OS to Windows 11, along with UEFI firmware and a TPM. If you’ve built a Windows 11 VM, you may already be running Q35 without realizing it.

Steam streaming on Proxmox doesn't require GPU passthrough, and my LXC setup proves it

It's not as weird as it sounds, honest

7
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Why you shouldn't flip every VM to Q35

It's not always necessary

With all of that in mind, it's tempting to open every VM you run and switch it over now, but you shouldn't. At least, not without a plan as to why.

On Linux, the usual casualty is networking in an active VM. Most modern distributions name network interfaces based on where they sit on the bus, and that changes with the new layout. An interface called ens18 can come back as something like enp6s18, and if your network configuration still points at the old name, the VM boots without an IP address. Windows can be fussier still and may need repair work after the switch, and while neither is really hard to fix, both are annoying on a VM that was working fine beforehand.

That's probably why Proxmox hasn't changed the default, because a VM without an explicit type set just uses the default, so changing it would just swap every VM that was created without one.

I built a $15 ESP32 display that shows exactly what my home server is doing

The missing piece wasn’t another monitor.

By  Shekhar Vaidya

Leave the machine type alone unless you need it

Seeing a 1996 chipset in your VM’s settings is a little jarring, but i440FX isn’t Proxmox neglecting to update a dropdown or a hefty performance sacrifice in the name of compatibility. It is for the sake of compatibility, but it works best out of the box for virtually all operating systems, and the parts that matter for performance have nothing to do with the VM's chipset.

item.title: A major decomp tool is shutting down after a tidal wave of AI: "The community aspect of decompilation has been broken"
item.itunes:title: A major decomp tool is shutting down after a tidal wave of AI: "The community aspect of decompilation has been broken"
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • LLM tools let anyone decompile and recompile games, enabling easy native ports.
  • Decomp.dev shut down after a deluge of LLM-made decompilations broke community trust.
  • Hostile AI forks and rushed, half-baked releases undermined cooperative projects.

AI coding has hit a tipping point where people can now perform native ports of games. Anyone can pick up an AI coding tool, ask it to decompile a game's source code, then recompile it so it can be ported anywhere they like. Unfortunately, it seems this new era of AI has taken its toll, as a major decomp community website has shut down amid the wave of LLM submissions.

Decomp.dev closes its doors after a deluge of LLM-made decomps

AI was causing issues with the initiative

Credit: Nintendo / Microsoft

As spotted by GamesRadar, the decomp.dev website has closed its doors. In a statement, the website states that the website's original goal was to "gamify decompilation." The idea was that ongoing decomp projects would have a little progress bar, which would encourage people to get excited about decomps, get involved with projects, and help people get games to more people.

However, with the recent surge in LLM-based decomps, the statement claims that the community spirit behind these projects has been "broken" for a few reasons:

Forking existing decompilation projects to "finish" them with AI.

Every project works differently: some may not want to use AI for legal or ethical reasons, and others may be okay with AI, or use AI themselves, but do not want drive-by contributions from folks who have put no effort into making sure the contributions are good. The bottom line is that these kinds of hostile forks put little to no effort into meaningfully contributing to existing projects, tearing apart our community fabric.

The statement also claims that people were using the website to 'race' human-made projects, where an AI user would grab the current work, then release it "half-baked" to take the credit for the release. Also, the site lists grievances with associating 'decomp' with specifically porting games to other platforms, as some enthusiasts just enjoy the challenge of 'cracking the code' without necessarily porting it anywhere.

Linus Torvalds used AI to fix a Linux bug, and now LLM critics on Linux face an uncomfortable choice

Avoiding software without AI code is getting very difficult.

27
By  Simon Batt

item.title: After a month with VS Code's new agents window, I stopped caring about Cursor
item.itunes:title: After a month with VS Code's new agents window, I stopped caring about Cursor
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve used VS Code for half a decade, but recently I’ve been switching between it and Cursor. VS Code is a good editor, but it lacks some of the agentic features that draw me to Cursor. I use Cursor extensively for development alongside Claude, and its own Composer models are quite good for coding. VS Code already supports agentic workflows through extensions like Claude Code and Codex, along with GitHub Copilot. You can get a lot done with these tools, but the overall experience hasn’t quite matched what I get from Cursor.

Microsoft’s dedicated Agents window closes much of that gap. It gives agent sessions their own space, with tools to manage work across projects and review changes. I can delegate tasks from this window and return to the regular editor when I need to work directly with the code. That brings many of the agentic features I use in Cursor into VS Code, giving me fewer reasons to leave the editor and extension ecosystem I’ve used for years.

I can keep my projects in one window

Switching between them is also easy

When you ask an agent to make changes, you spend more time following its work and answering questions. Cursor already has a dedicated interface for this workflow, and I like that VS Code now offers something similar without needing another extension.

I can start an agent session for one repository and open another for a different project without launching a separate VS Code window for each. Both sessions appear in the sidebar under their respective projects, along with their progress and whether they need input. You can leave one running and switch to the other, or open them side by side if you want to follow both. The files and terminal belong to the selected session, so switching projects also brings up the workspace associated with that conversation.

For example, you could have one agent fix a bug in one repository, and another add a feature to a different project. You don’t have to finish one conversation before starting the next or keep returning to separate editor windows to check on them. Cursor already offers this through its Agents Window, and having it in VS Code removes one reason I use a separate editor.

If both tasks involve the same repository, you can give each session its own Git worktree. This creates separate working copies where the agents can make changes without immediately touching the files in your main workspace. Opening two chats alone doesn’t provide that separation, since both can still edit the same files.

I thought I was productive in VS Code until agentic coding showed me what I was missing

The death of the traditional IDE.

9
By  Parth Shah

You can choose your agents and models

You don’t need to stick with what Microsoft offers

The best thing about VS Code's agent window is that you're not entirely at Microsoft's mercy. You can choose Copilot, Claude, or Codex as the harness for a session, with a separate selection of models available for each. Since I already use Claude alongside Cursor, I like having access to Anthropic’s agent harness within VS Code. Selecting a Claude model through Copilot still uses Copilot’s tools and agent workflow. Choosing the Claude harness uses Anthropic’s Agent SDK, including its supported tools and customizations.

You can then choose an available model based on the work you’re assigned. The selection depends on your harness, account, and configured providers. There’s also support for bringing your own model credentials, although BYOK in Agent Host sessions is still experimental. The session also includes controls for what the agent can do without asking you. You can configure approvals for supported tools and commands, and use project instructions to specify coding conventions or how changes should be tested. Those settings depend on the harness, so an existing configuration won’t necessarily work identically across all three.

Once the agent makes changes, you can open the diffs and leave feedback against a selected range of code. That lets you point directly to the implementation you want changed instead of copying it into another prompt and explaining where it belongs.

I have fewer reasons to leave VS Code

VS Code is now a complete platform

VS Code has been my go-to development tool, but I felt it lagged behind in AI features, even though Microsoft started calling it an open-source AI code editor long ago. It now feels like a complete platform thanks to the Agents window.

I compared VS Code, Cursor, and Google Antigravity for 30 days, and one pulled far ahead

One tool simply felt ahead.

item.title: An old Android tablet is the best universal remote I've ever owned
item.itunes:title: An old Android tablet is the best universal remote I've ever owned
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When you have multiple TVs in the house and you start to pair them with smart TV boxes, keeping track of it all can be a nightmare. Universal TV remotes used to be more popular when you just needed an IR transmitter and TV interfaces were simple, but these days, interfaces are more complex, and there's more to consider.

The solution is quite simple, though. An old Android tablet I don't use anymore quickly became everything I needed to control my TVs with next to gaps in functionality. And I wouldn't have it any other way.

You don't need an IR transmitter

TVs are all internet-connected now

In the past, for your phone to be a universal TV remote, you'd need it to be one of the rare examples of a phone with a built-in IR transmitter. These days, though, the majority of TVs can connect to the internet, and you can use any phone to control them.

You can find multiple universal remote control apps on your favorite app store that let you take advantage of this capability and control all the TVs in your home relatively easily. I found this particular app from BoostVision to be the most functional on a tablet. A lot of these apps also seem to be designed for smaller phone screens, but this one adjusts pretty well to the larger tablet display.

With my LG TV, I can use D-pad controls or a virtual touchpad to move the on-screen pointer, but I also get volume buttons, quick navigation controls, and even access to my app list, so I can immediately jump into any app I want without navigating the UI on the TV itself. It's very useful. The big gap here is the ability to turn the TV on.

I turned my Android phone into a TV remote with this free app

If you're looking for a simple TV remote app, Bluetooth Remote is the best around.

6
By  Patrick O'Rourke

I wasn't able to find a free app with Wake-on-LAN support, so I still need to turn the TV on using the physical remote. Sadly, most of these apps can also be a bit slow to load, but the functionality is there, and it's very helpful.

Both of my TVs are LG-branded, but they are from different generations, and they run very different versions of webOS, and they both work just fine. I would imagine you can just as easily use a Samsung TV or any other brand, too.

See at Google Play Store

It goes great with self-hosting, too

Home Assistant is the true universal remote

While you can use one of the many Play Store apps to control your TV remotely, I have to say that Home Assistant is easily the best way to control my TVs. The flip side to this is that deploying Home Assistant if you haven't already, plus configuring the necessary integrations, can take a lot more work than simply grabbing a Play Store app.

In the case of my LG models, I had to grab this project from the Home Assistant community, which gives me a full remote control for each of my TVs. Because I can fully customize the UI, I was able to squeeze two of these remotes onto the same page, so I can control either the bedroom TV or the living room TV without going back and forth in the UI. Plus, much like some of the dedicated apps, I can instantly jump into a specific app or input source without wading through slow TV menus. In that sense, it's actually much better than using a real remote.

The devices are also saved and the remotes are always shown, so I don't have to reconnect every time, and Home Assistant is also faster to load. With some extra configuration work, I can also get Wake-on-LAN support, though admittedly, I've only been able to get this to work with my bedroom TV, not the older model in my living room. I've heard this can work better if the TV is wired instead of using Wi-Fi, though I can't test this.

I revived a cheap Android tablet by turning it into a Home Assistant control panel

Your old Android tablet is a better Home Assistant panel than anything you can buy

2
By  Ayush Pande

There's also a way to add an Android TV remote to Home Assistant, but this is something I admittedly haven't tried to do since it seems fairly complex. Other similar projects exist to help enable remote controls for other brands of TV, so it's worth exploring. That being said, this is a much more complex way to go about enabling remote controls, so I wouldn't blame you for sticking with the simpler solutions above.

At the same time, Home Assistant can control much more than TVs, so there are plenty of reasons to check it out.

Android TV has its own app

Sticking with something trusted

As I've already hinted, the apps above can also control an Android TV-based box like the one in my living room, but for Android TV, I think the official Google Home app is the best way to go. So, to control my Chromecast with Google TV, I added Google's Home app to my tablet as well.

The controls on the Google Home app are kind of basic, but I can do pretty much anything I want to do, and even if I didn't want to use the tablet as a standard remote, Android TV often asks me to use my phone if I want to type into any text field, so being able to do that on the same device makes things a lot easier.

Google Home also adds the currently playing media to my Android notifications, so I can easily play and pause, or even adjust the volume, even while I'm using other apps. All things considered, it's great.

My tablet is more useful than ever

I've often seen it said that every one must learn for themselves how useless a tablet can be, but by combining a couple of apps, I've found a new kind of purpose for this old tablet, and it now belongs right in my living room. Whether it's the TVs themselves or the set-top box I have in the living room, my tablet does it all, and I highly recommend trying this out for yourself if you have an old tablet lying around.

The solution is quite simple, though. An old Android tablet I don't use anymore quickly became everything I needed to control my TVs with next to gaps in functionality. And I wouldn't have it any other way.

You don't need an IR transmitter

TVs are all internet-connected now

In the past, for your phone to be a universal TV remote, you'd need it to be one of the rare examples of a phone with a built-in IR transmitter. These days, though, the majority of TVs can connect to the internet, and you can use any phone to control them.

I found this particular app from BoostVision to be the most functional on a tablet. A lot of these apps also seem to be designed for smaller phone screens, but this one adjusts pretty well to the larger tablet display.

The controls on the Google Home app are kind of basic, but I can do pretty much anything I want to do, and even if I didn't want to use the tablet as a standard remote, Android TV often asks me to use my phone if I want to type into any text field, so being able to do that on the same device makes things a lot easier.
